This paper examines the deformation of G₂-instantons within a fixed nearly G₂ structure, demonstrating how linearized conditions for these instantons are equivalent to Bianchi identities of associated neutral curvature 2-forms. Based on this equivalence, we establish a deformation theorem that extends work by Ková\u00efs, showing the result is optimal within an optimal sense. Our proof integrates multiple approaches: identifying G₂-instantons as solutions to a system of gradient flows, utilizing a specific identification with SO(4)-instantsons on a 6-dimensional hyperkähler space, and employing a technique from \u0161evri\u00f6k's recent research that might prove generally useful.

Point Clouds, which consist of discrete 3D coordinates, have emerged as a prominent format for representing unstructured geometric shapes, particularly in vision tasks. To handle this discreteness, standard practices involve mapping raw data to continuous spaces using deep neural networks followed by smoothing operations to approximate the underlying surface. However, current smoothing techniques are constrained by the specific 3D representation—such as SIGMA-Normal or PFH features—resulting in noisy, imprecise, and sometimes inaccurate geometric estimates. We introduce Smoothing via Transformation-dependency-Closure (SMTCL), a novel point cloud smoothing method that generates high-fidelity representation smoothing independent of input 3D formats, significantly outperforming existing approaches. Crucially, SMTCL does not rely on pre-training or additional training; it is applicable to both supervised learning and self-supervised learning, as well as learning-by-acquisition. Experimental results across multiple 3D representation learning settings demonstrate SMTCL's superiority over current state-of-the-art methods. Source code and datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI

This paper investigates medium access control protocols tailored for Frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar networks. It contrasts the performance of two approaches—slotted ALOHA and CSMA. The slotted ALOHA method is evaluated in both single and dual-antenna configurations, analyzing key metrics such as the probability of successful packet transmission, throughput, and mean waiting time. In the CSMA section, we present a theoretical analysis of collision probability by examining interference range and transmission distance as functions of the Chirp bandwidth sweep rate. Subsequently, we introduce a suboptimal sensing approach designed to minimize collision risks and analyze its impact on radar network lifetime. Subsequently, numerical results are provided to validate the proposed theoretical findings and comparisons between the different sludge ALOHA approaches are also discussed in the context of overall system performance.

While Hong-Ou-Mou (Hong) interference is classically understood as an optical nonlinearity manifesting as complete absorbance, we propose and validate a framework where non-linear photon absorption processes are reinterpreted as positive and negative absorption events. Within this model, We introduce the Entangled Two-Photon Absorption (ETPA), defined as the absorption of a photon pair through a single linear absorption event. Initially, we demonstrate that when two-photon absorption occurs within a thin optical medium, it produces a complete suppression of transmitted light analogous to 100% nonlinearity. Furthermore, we show the feasibility of optical amplification by positioning the source behind such a medium. Subsequently, we explore various linear absorption mechanisms, specifically ETPA, that generate distinct signatures in Hong interference patterns. These predictions have been experimentally confirmed using thulium-doped crystal materials.

This paper calculates the reduced circle-equivariant logical elliptic cohomology of projective spaces $\CP(V)$ for a complex vector space $V$. This computation yields a specific instance within the broader category of equivariant cohomology theories of projective spaces. Consequently, findings from this study are applicable to other theories that fall inside or map equivariant $K$-theory and Kwyierian cohomology.

Temporal Knowledge Graph Inference (TKGI) aims to forecast missing subject, object, or temporal markers within knowledge graphs that incorporate timing data. As TKGI is pivotal for various applications ranging from recommending systems to medical drug discovery, research efforts have largely favored low-computation Linear Time Evolving (LTE) models. Although these models offer computational efficiency, the constraint of linearity degrades performance on complex datasets. To overcome this, we introduce a hybrid representation learning architecture that integrates both low-rank and model-independent approaches. During training, we implement an inductive step to reduce model parameters by leveraging K-means clustering on latent embeddings, thereby enabling parameter-efficient learning. Empirical evaluations indicate that this framework surpasse both state-of-the-art models (such as TAIL/TORK) as well as established baseline methods (including TBPE/TGBN) on complex datasets like CWKGO and CKGD while retaining lower computational complexity.

In ground source heat pump systems, a vertical U-tube ground heat exchange is typically buried. The surrounding soil noise significantly affects the heat exchange process, yet previous research has paid little attention to it, frequently assuming the ground noise is uniform and equal to the average value. This paper employs the two-dimensional numerical simulation of a single U-tube model to show that, far from the tube, ground noise gradients are negligible, effectively making it one-dimensional there. The numerical findings are then benchmarked against analytical predictions based on the Heat Conduction Periodic Response (HCPR) model. We further utilize the heat defect coefficient, a parameter often used in heat defect calculations. The results indicate that ignoring ground noise, or assuming it is uniformly distributed as an average,{'result': 'significantly misjudges the U-tube performance, often leading issues that are not addressed by these assumptions.

While quantum non-Bound entangled (QBE) states are non-entangled according to standard entropy-based measures, they can demonstrate Bell nonlocality by violating Bell inequalities. In this work, we show that idealized correlations—conceptually similar to those required for "finely-tuned" violations of Bell inequalities—can prove Bell nonlocality without relying on inequalities, but only for QBE states when examined through non-projective measurements and non-ideal quantum correlations. Finding ideal correlations practical is challenging; however, we demonstrate here that despite deviations, the class of QBE remains capable of showcasing Bell-Bell nonlocality without inequalities under fine-tuned conditions if one considers generalized measurements and the imperfections inherent to the state.

"Flat bands are commonly associated with localized or highly non-uniform wave functions; however, we demonstrate that they can also arise in highly diffusive, uniformly distributed quantum states. This counterintuitive behavior stems from near-degenerate Landau levels induced by a disordered magnetic field. Our findings, supported by numerical simulations, contrast sharply with the prevailing consensus found in optical lattice systems, where flat bands typically trigger localization. Instead, we propose that flat bands in systems with disordered magnetic fields drive confining behaviors typical of localized states in standard optical lattice models. Consequently, we advocate for utilizing magnetic fields as a mechanism to access flat-band physics without the inherent complexities and limitations of constructing flat-band models within optical lattices."

Metals containing B, such as NaB, were predicted by theoretical models to exhibit superconductivity at high temperatures. Here, we report density functional theory computations suggesting that at 200 GPa, the NaB metal could reach a critical temperature ($T_c$) of approximately 90 K. However, we argue that the pressure magnitude is unreasonably high, as the proposed superconducting phase relies on ionic vibrations that are not present in a purely electronic framework. We present evidence indicating that, under more realistic pressure ranges, hydrogen boride fails to demonstrate notable superconducting properties.

When working with N-dimensional section arrays under the "doall" assumption, it is often necessary to apply an operation across every section. Executing this operation in an ordered, nested loop structure—such as traversing sections via loop indices $i$ for dimension $dim_i$ within the range of available sections—is only optimal for N dimensions if those loops are fully parallelized. If even a single loop lacks parallelization, the overall algorithm becomes suboptimal. To address this, the paper proposes Xdflat, a runtime framework designed around explicit parallel looping constructs that facilitate efficient traversal of sections. The framework ensures that every loop initiated by this approach achieves full parallelization across all known dimensions. Furthermore, it enables algorithms originally dependent on N nested loops to scale efficiently across an $(N+1)$-dimensional space. The authors detail the architecture supporting these capabilities and present empirical benchmarks demonstrating its performance. These tests illustrate that the Xdflat approach delivers several orders of magnitude speedup compared to traditional, implicitly parallelized nested loop implementations.

We investigate $\Gamma$-maps originating from a free group where the arithmetic group $\Gamma$ features finite vertex-stabilizers within a general locally finite simplicial complex. By adapting concepts from dynamics and quasi-chemistry, we define and examine two central properties: charm and readability (or rigidity). We establish that for many arithmetic groups, particularly classical ones, the presence of a non-abelian finitely generated normal subgroup is both a necessary and sufficient condition for the space to be charming. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when $\Gamma$ is a nice arithmetic group and acts faithfully on a contractible, locally finite, simply-connected simplicial complex with finite edge-stabilizers, the action exhibits rigidity under specific geometric constraints.

Drive-by-wire and automation Level 5 systems harness computational capabilities to oversee vehicle operations, enabling use cases ranging from highway driving to complex urban environments. These scenarios present substantial challenges in fault management, as real-world conditions introduce a wide variety of failures not easily replicable during standard testing. While fault diversification strategies can shift how errors manifest and lead to novel system behaviors, current industry approaches lack the tools to verify their efficacy. This report demonstrates the application of model-based fault detection and isolation with reconfiguration (FDI/MFA) within a car-following scenario to validate a fail-functional design. Using industry-accepted parameters and statistical fault models to simulate highway conditions, the study confirms that a properly deployed FDI scheme can ensure the driving system achieves fail-safe status through reliable reconfiguration following the initial failure and the presence of multiple potential defects.

Many real-world systems are nonlinear and intricate. Recent years have seen significant progress in using machine learning to analyze such complex and adaptive behaviors. This study introduces a novel approach for grouping dynamical systems based on their predicted impacts from specific perturbations. Our method employs a fully convolutional neural network to learn dynamical embeddings, which enable the algorithm to capture both spatial and temporal dynamics. These embeddings facilitate a fully automatic, state-dependent clustering process. This data-driven framework can be applied to reduce complex high-dimensional state spaces by identifying submanifolds that retain long-term system dynamics. As a practical demonstration, this new algorithm successfully clusters and simplifies the state spaces of the Chua circuit, a robotic arm configuration, and the 16-ball table.

This paper explores how modern approaches in nonstandard analysis, smooth infinitesimal geometry, and Robinson's concepts can reconstruct the methods of Leibnizian calculus. We argue that smooth infinitesimal geometry offers the most suitable framework for explaining these historical techniques, specifically highlighting the differential ideal approach as particularly promising. In constructing the idealized calculus, we adhere closely to historical principles, with special emphasis on representing variables as dual numbers in $\mathbb R[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2=0)$.

Although intensity mapping represents a promising new technique for observing large-scale neutral hydrogen (HI) distributions, current interferometric implementations face significant disturbances caused by the observer's local environment, such as nearby trees, power lines, and radio telescopes. These disturbances introduce coherent artifacts that can obscure cosmological signals. This study demonstrates how various background rejection methods can be evaluated using realistic disturbances by analyzing them with disturbance theory calculations. We find that while simple on-off deposition cannot remove the coherent nature of interference, more advanced approaches, like beamformed tomographic imaging, effectively suppress these artifacts. Furthermore, our results suggest that even with perfect background rejection, power from radio sources will dominate intensity map data, surpassing the HI cosmological signal by orders of magnitude by 2025. To address this, we propose a method for isolating the HI signal through its unique angular power spectrum signature, an approach we validate using both disturbance theory simulations and Monte Carlo simulations.

This study establishes the equivalence between three features of mathematical objects: (i) the ability to approximate a specific type of transformation using finite-dimensional systems (characterized here as a "self-scalable" state for self-amplitude收缩); (ii) possessing unlimited dimension; and (iii) possessing operator-based representations that span an infinite sequence of matrix operations that can be truncated at will to achieve desired accuracy. This equivalence is demonstrated first through quantum computing systems and then extended more broadly to classical autonomous systems of any dimension and type. By confirming these trichotomies, the paper reveals four interconnected ways in which these autonomous systems autonomy function as mutually exclusive yet theoretically identical concepts.

This work addresses the challenge of recommending diverse items to users by combining complementary approaches. We designed a new method, ActiveHybridRec, which integrates feedback-driven behavioral rules with content-driven documentation to create user profiles. Unlike many hybrid models that simply re-rank items from multiple algorithms, our approach utilizes document context to enhance learned user representations. Specifically, we merge user representations with item attributes by analyzing our data and interpreting how the users' query documents reflect their preferences. We also incorporate the concept of user agency by designing an interactive interface that allows individuals to actively select recommendations. Experimental results using three real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms both existing hybrid recommender systems and standard baseline algorithms.

This work explores two topics regarding random matrices: the derivation of necessary and sufficient conditions for freeness of kind $B$ and an exploration of conditional independence. To establish sufficient conditions for freeness of kind $B$, the authors employ free Hilbert space-valued conditional expectations along with a technique conditioning on a subalgebra generated by a single matrix. Regarding conditional independence, two distinct approaches are analyzed: one conditionals matrices independent of a fixed unitary matrix, and another independent of random unitaries. It is demonstrated that these strategies suffice to derive independence among matrices that possess transformationally invariant distributions

This paper introduces a novel observation model tailored for automated planning with explicit timing (ATP). Unlike previous approaches that infer observations only upon reaching specific states within the environment, our framework permits observations at any step. It defines a relation connecting ATP solutions to agent observations, determined by which states are observable and the associated noise level. Framework constraints limit this planning structure to ensure calculable, compact, and dense observation sequences relative to an agent's path. Merely satisfying these requirements would be impossible for general observation functions and ATP structures, thus these constraints may force a particular formulation of observations or path-related problem restrictions. Consequently, agents must infer environments and goal states through their planning processes based on noisy data acquired over multiple steps. While designed for broader applications, implementation is feasible only with limited contexts or by adopting an "implicit" noise model, which links observation noise directly to Nondeterministic Automatic Planning (NAT) problems. In such scenarios, each solution to an ATP task corresponds uniquely and directly to one non-pluralistic agent trajectory, aligning specific environments and goal configurations with singular observation sequences.

Utilizing the framework of hadronic molecular models, we investigate the $\bar{B}_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0\eta$ transition, with a particular focus on the potential $s$-wave contribution arising from the intermediate state $J/\psi a_0(1450)$. Our analysis indicates that the $\eta$ meson exhibits a predominant $u\bar{u}, d\bar{d}, \text{and} s\bar{s}$ composition within the $a_0(1450)$ component. Additionally, the study clarifies the nature of the near-degenerate $a_0(1450)-f_0(1450)$ system by demonstrating the significant role of gluonic components in the nonet structure. These outcomes enable a precise determination of the $a_0(1450)-f_0(1450)$ mixing angle.

We introduce a method handling the resolution of multivariate polynomial systems where data contains stochastic errors. Residing in the positive quadrants, the target solutions are characterized as the cluster exhibiting minimum norm within the support of posterior distributions. To enhance computational performance, we propose an early stopping criterion capable of detecting an optimal cessation point when solving these systems via iterative algorithms on stochastic data. Under the assumption of conditional independence across measurement errors, criteria derived specifically for use with iterative resolution algorithms are proposed, proving their validity through application to well-known resolution strategies such as Algebraic Reconstruction Techniques (ART) and the Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique (SIRT).

This study presents a novel method involving the parimetrically symmetric release of electron-positron pairs from gold nanoparticles embedded in ethanol under a high-intensity pulsed infrared field. The process utilizes radiation-induced charge separation inside the nanoparticle; however, the posetronic emission is achieved via a two-step mechanism governed by the internal electric field and external laser radiation. This symmetry-based approach ensures a balanced emission of positive and negative charges. A critical advantage of this technique is the anticipation of nearly null net charge accumulation within the particle, thereby minimizing adverse interactions with surrounding quantum objects. Furthermore, the research outlines principles for generating complex quantic configurations—including charge-neutral systems containing large numbers of electron-positron pairs—by carefully controlling release parameters. Ultimately, the proposed parameter-dependent parity-symmetry bundle emission opens new avenues for research in nanoscale quantum biology and quantum chemistry.

We introduce a straightforward and accurate analytical model for thermodynamics of equilibrium alkali gases. In this study, we examine atom radiation and electron-phonon interactions alongside radiation and electron exchange at surfaces. These mechanisms lead various gases to deviate from standard behavior, even in cases where the Grotthus-Rushbrooke rule seems applicable. Consequently, traditional theories often yield inaccurate estimates for alkali metals due to their dual nature of behaving like both ideal and non-ideal gases. By modeling these complex interactions, we derive analytical expressions for the heat capacities, thermal conductivities, and the relationship between pressure and specific volume. For gases in equilibrium between excited and unexcited states, we further investigate how specific volume influences molar heat capacity and thermal conductivity. The resulting calculations for the heat capacities and pressure-specific volume relationships in equilibrium lithium gas demonstrate excellent agreement with existing experimental data.

This paper investigates the environment of vector mesons during the early stages of high-energy heavy-ion interactions. Utilizing the effective Lagrangial method based on a vacuum populated by particles and incorporating a medium-exhibited chiral discrepancy, we analyze key properties of the medium-exhibited mass modification, width alteration, in-medium trajectory, and decay temperature of vector mesons. Our findings reveal a medium-exhibited mass reduction stemming from two sources: (1) the influence of a medium-exhibited medium-exhibited medium-exhibited mass, (2) An effective Ladder mass. Furthermore, we observe that the medium modifies its width and trajectory. Specifically, at lower momentum values, the width exhibits dependence on medium-exhibited medium-exhibited discrepancy; at higher values, it is primarily dictated by the density of the medium. Additionally, at elevated density, both the trajectory in the complex plane and decay temperature are driven by a medium-exhibited discrepancy.

Small-world networks are defined by a low average path length, which is typically approximated using either global or local weak clearing times. T he problem of estimating these time scales even in the presence up to $f<\frac{n}{2}$ arbitrary faults (Byzantine) in an $n$ node node system is addressed. A novel algorithm, which operates within $\mathcal{O}(f\log^2n)$ nodes and exhibits a high resilience against up to $o(\frac{n}{2})$ arbitrary nodes, yields an $\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{2})$ approximation ratio. If the fault nodes are assumed fixed rather than arbitrary (the "static" problem), any set of up to $\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{2})$ nodes can be removed with a high probability while requiring only $\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{2})$ nodes and no additional time from them.

This paper presents a new methodology designed to generate binary neutron star (BNS) data sets for testing and validating general relativistic hydrodynamics (GRH) solvers. While BNS systems are a primary source of signals for gravitational-wave detectors, existing BNS datasets are limited, hindering the rigorous evaluation of GRH solvers across diverse conditions. Our approach employs a BNS parameter space sampling technique that systematically varies variables such as magnetic field strength, initial fluid setup, BSSN implementation choices, and numerical methods. These variations ensure BNS simulations cover a broad spectrum of gravitational-wave sources. By offering comprehensive diversity in initial conditions, we aim to substantially improve the ability of researchers to conduct thorough systematic tests of their GRH solvers. Consequently, this framework will foster wider GRH self-assessment within the gravitational-wave community and better prepare them for the arrival of the LIGO-Virgo-KGEO (LIGO-Virgo-KGEO) detector network.

The principal objective of the JUNO project, a collaboration led from Zhongshan, China, involves constructing a large-scale liquid scintillator detector aimed at elucidating neutrino flavor oscillations in the context of reactor antineutrino and antiproton interactions. Precise measurement of the Cherenkov ring imagery produced by these oscillations is fundamental to JUNO’s scientific mission, which critically depends on employing 20-inch diameter photomultiplier tubes (PMTs). These massive tubes, sourced from Hamamatsu,atsu, comprise a total inventory of 7,600 units. Photomultiplier tube performance hinges on several variables, most significantly the lead glass-type and PMT structural elements like dynodes and photocathodes used. To ensure optimal scientific outcomes from JUNO's design, every single PMT must be evaluated for performance, which necessitates extensive optical characterization of each individual detector component. In this report, an advanced methodology used to evaluate 2-inch diameter PMTs is presented, which integrates advanced Monte-Carlo simulations (using GEANT-4 framework) alongside experimental procedures to ensure high-quality results for JUNO's scientific mission by meticulously evaluating PMT components through both theoretical modeling and practical application. This report details how this hybrid technique enables precise examination of 2-inch diameter photomultiplier tubes within JUNO's scope.

Predicting multivariate temporal data is essential across numerous fields but remains difficult due to the presence of noise and dependencies across diverse time scales. Although many algorithms have been developed to address this issue, existing methods typically assume a fixed network architecture, failing to detect interactions within high-dimensional data or capture varying dependencies on different time horizons. This study introduces AGCN, a novel adaptive multi-scale approach that jointly learns both network topology and output structures for forecasting tasks. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical framework for evaluating the proposed method and validate its performance through rigorous experiments comparing it to state-of-the-art baselines across six real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that AGCN consistently outperforms these baselines, showing particular superiority in predicting short-term scenarios.

This study examines scattering phenomena in the solar disk and its immediate atmosphere using on-sky data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory's Atmospheric Imaging Instruments (SDI/AIA). The primary aim is to assess existing solar models by comparing them with observational data, with results indicating that a model consisting of four layers provides superior equivalence to the measurements across all instruments compared to more complex alternatives. Furthermore, we explore how to optimize simple solar models for better representativeness, achieving significant improvements through the application of Bayesian methods combined with genetic algorithms.

Pre-trained language models have emerged as vital assets in NLP; however, their massive architecture and computationally heavy nature necessitate the shift toward pre-distributed platforms for knowledge transfer. While knowledge distillation offers a solution by shifting learning loads to the student, the requirement for a unified integrated knowledge system in such models remains the challenge. This paper introduces a multi-instructor framework designed to learn from diverse knowledge sources simultaneously. We propose Pairwise Iterative Logits Election (PILE) to construct an effective teacher stack by iteratively assessing the relational dynamics and interplay among various students. Evaluation on the Google Bigbird-ROPE platform demonstrates that PILE enables efficient training with a significantly smaller network compared to competitive approaches, achieving comparable performance on the TURL challenge while maintaining efficiency.

The discovery of dark energy and the possibility of the Higgs boson suggest that the Standard Model is incomplete, likely because new physics operates at extremely low energy scales. Recent theoretical and experimental progress has spurred fresh interest in searching for ultralight bosonic dark matter fields, which could exhibit oscillating effects within this framework. Alongside the recently enhanced atomic clocks that push measurement precision even further, the authors introduce a novel "strength" interferometry technique. This method aims to detect dark field variations by measuring shifts in fine-structure constants, offering significant potential for confirming the existence of such new physics under a quantum field theory paradigm, along with unique benefits over existing approaches.

Match-wide features are increasingly integral to modern packet processors, extending basic functionality beyond standard actions. While standard operations involve processing data at specific locations identified by exact or precise matches, P16 enables the definition of actions triggered by any portion of a packet. An adaptable packet classifier is fundamental to a diverse range of applications, extending from IP Next Generation (IPv6), WPA3, and CONIC5 to TCP stacks. However, integrating these advanced packet-processing capabilities demands substantial P16 program complexity. We present an open-source P16 program-translation tool, which simplifies the development of packet-processing applications by unifying three core components: a standardizable matcher/processor, shared programs, an extensible match-box, and an extensible program library.

The magnitude of $\boldsymbol q\cdot\boldsymbol n$ integrated across any mesh face $F$ represents the net volumetric flow through that face. For any control volume $K$, the discrepancy between the sum of these summed interfacial fluxes and the negative change in stored volume ($\partial_t$) within $K$ yields a balance error. This study evaluates the precision of $\boldsymbol q$ numerically computed via Raviart-Thomas finite elements of minimal order on general quadrilateral grids. We demonstrate that when the local mesh exhibits only slight aspect ratios, a precise balance error should theoretically vanish. However, the application of standard numerical quadrature introduces an additional error term that can be adjusted by adopting a specific, non-conventional quadration rule. Implementing this modified approach for the flux computation ensures a near-exact satisfaction of every local water balance equation.

Federated Learning (FL) enables secure collaboration among distributed parties to train a model without exposing their local data. Current FL frameworks struggle with rigorous privacy guarantees, as data movement between nodes exposes information about the moving sets. Our work demonstrates that Unique Identifiers泄露 more than just participation status—specifically, it leaks the exact joining and departing timestamps for each data contributor, an detail unprotected by existing solutions. We establish a Strong Differential Privacy framework adapted for FL, named Unique Identifiers Confidentiality (IC), ensuring that movements are concealed effectively even under adversarial observation. Our main achievement is FedUCI, a novel decentralized system built around an efficient, dynamic group testing protocol designed to satisfy IC requirements. This framework allows nodes to remain anonymous regarding their data migration activities. Beyond strong individual privacy, we show that achieving this level of confidentiality also enhances overall training fairness by mitigating the bias often introduced by strategic user joining and departure patterns.

We introduce an explicit continuous-phase Runge-Kutta scheme designed for solving ordinary differential equations. Correspondingly, we derive the associated Runge-Kutta method with stepped integration. Utilible order condition concepts applicable to this continuous-phase formulation are established. Finally, applicable scenarios for achieving high asymptotic efficiency are examined.

Creating Efficient Artificial Intelligence systems demands both high-performance hardware and well-optimized software; however, current development tools often lack adequate support for the increasingly complex and computationally heavy software architectures, particularly in the realm of deep learning. Our work introduces a softwar e hardware co-design framework designed for large-scale, regionally evaluated training. We demonstrate an implementation where software modules are distributed across multiple regions, each equipped with its own processing resources. Within this setup, a dedicated evaluator resides in every region to monitor local compute activities and adapt software behavior accordingly. Hardare in each region is specialized for distinct deep-learning tasks, while a software model harmonizes the code across all regions. Our hardware was built on a many-core architecture featuring 128 ARM Cortex-A72 processors and 4 DSPs per region. We evaluated this setup using a ResNet-50 software architecture across 3 such regions with 3 input data channels, comparing results against an unoptimized baseline. While this linear-magnetics response is generally negligible, it may become pronounced and exhibit distinct behaviors during a transition across the integer boundary of the topological index. Assessing the interaction risks between medications is critical for patient safety, yet this is severely hindered by the massive volume of paired data and domain expertise that remain unutilized. Currently, although machine learning (ML) techniques have a limited track record in this field, they show significant potential for harnessing such abundant information and knowledge. We call this the Cohesive Perspective for Deep Learning on Medication Pairs (CP-DPM). Functioning as a unified model, CP-DPM can be employed either as a standalone system for initial screening or as a transferable component to improve other safety models. Identifying road hazards such as potholes is crucial for public safety, a reason why automated detection through algorithms has become a critical research focus. This study introduces a transfer learning approach designed to identify harmful road features across diverse countries, even when using camera sensors with varying characteristics. Our methodology employs a sequential transfer strategy: first, a model is pre-trained on hazardous data from a specific target country to create a specialized base model; subsequently, this base model is transferred to a second distinct country for the fine-tuning of the final detector. This process iterates across all target locations. Evaluations conducted over six unique nations demonstrate the system's efficacy, achieving an average Intersection over Union (IoU) of 81.6% across all locations. Furthermore, since achieving 79.1% average IoU on the initial target country required only one-tenth the dataset size compared to pre-training in that specific location, our method is also highly data-efficient.

Statewide mandates requiring the treatment of incarcerated individuals have increased in recent years; however, there is limited understanding regarding this intervention's impact on such individuals' mental health. Federated learning (FL) offers a robust framework for securely collaborating on model training. In the process known as Federated Averaging, clients transmit locally trained model updates to a central server, which merges them into a new global model for the subsequent round. While this approach supports various optimization methods, such as using momentum, it often suffers from specific challenges. This paper demonstrates that the gradient of Federated Averaging is unconstrained, causing both client-level updates and server-level parameters to overshoot optimal values excessively. Key challenges in constructing Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs) include labor-intensive, error-prone annotation costs. We introduce a model-based approach for predicting unannotated facts in TKGs to support this process. Existing literature on knowledge graph completion (KGC) relies on linking specific head or tail items to probabilistic entities using parameter-rich models; however, prior research indicates that fixed model architectures suitable for TKGs have not yet been explored. Furthermore, pre-populated TKGs remain scarce, necessitating predictions on partially completed graphs. We present a framework utilizing fixed model structures to perform factual prediction directly. This method demonstrates prior to annotation that fact prediction outperforms entity prediction in precision. Additionally, the approach identifies missing data with greater accuracy in pre-annotated TCGs than in Temporal Knowledge Graphs. The study provides the first benchmark for comparing multiple models across various fixed structures within the context of missing fact detection.

This research addresses the determination of conditions under which shift equivalence between directed graphs leads to matrix equivalence, specifically in instances involving rows that are not finitely constrained. We establish such criteria to prove that for graphs with rows not containing infinitely many elements, robust shift equivalence generates Morita equivalence of their associated right stochastically generated $C^*$-algebras. Consequently, these findings extend to infinite algebraic systems governed by similar graph representations.

Given an Artin module $V$ over $\mathbb{Q}_p$, we define the $\mathscr{L}$-invariant $\text{L}(V)$, which serves as a $p$-adic rational number (or $\infty$) capable of filling a void left by the De Rham period when $V$ fails to satisfy the condition of being "de Rham." We demonstrate that this invariant remains consistent across various equivalent formulations and investigate its behavior under short exact sequences, notably establishing a specific $\mathscr{L}$-invariant for the quotient of two Iwasawa modules that enables us to derive relationships between $\text{L}$-invariants of such systems. These findings yield a new, independent formula relating the De Rham periods and $p$-adic $L$-functions associated with Hida families and their specializations, offering a distinct verification alongside previous proofs by Bennequin, Bertolini--Nekovar--Schoof, and Wan.

Detecting multiband microwave and terahertz radiation emitted by quantum materials and devices is essential for characterizing their electrodynamic properties. Conventional absorption-based detection methods require scanning with tuned devices, a process that becomes prohibitively slow when the frequency range is high. To address this, we demonstrate a gigahertz-wide microwave detector utilizing radiofrequency (RF) spectroscopy on a native Rydberg atom sensor within a microwave imaging system, achieving simultaneous coverage of 40 distinct frequencies across a 10 GHz span. Our results indicate that a real-time scanning strategy using a single static frequency yields spatial resolution and signal-to-noise ratios that rival or exceed those obtained through "scanning" via frequency multiplexing. Finally, we illustrate how a convolutional neural network trained on Rydberg detection data can automate the extraction of local voltage amplitudes and phases from spectrograms, thereby minimizing the impact of noise and computational scan time on data analysis.

This work presents early LBT/GT8 observations of UGC 8839, a nearby spiral galaxy, aimed at developing high-precision, high-resolution maps of the kinematic and positional fields. The primary goal is to identify the ultra-stable rigidly rotating massive disk characteristic of well-behaved galaxies. Our kinematic analysis reveals a substantial, rigidly rotating component extending to approximately $R \sim 5.5$ kpc, which corresponds to an outer mass-to-light ratio of $\sim5.5$ and yields a mass of $\sim10^{11} \mathrm{M_{\odot}}$. The ACS/UVIT UVM2 photometry indicates that stellar populations are young and blue, with ages around $10^8$ years, suggesting recent starbursts in galaxies of this galaxy type. When comparing the GT8 velocity maps to those anticipated from a simple two-component model (stellar matter plus a black hole), the residuals are minimal. This agreement implies that UGC 8839 hosts a small supermassive black hole, likely less than $10^8 \mathrm{M_{\odot}}$ in mass. As a supplement to the mass-constrained mean value property introduced by Kuusi, Zakharyaschev, and the author in \cite{AZZ}, we introduce a specific measure that characterizes quasiregularity. We prove two mass-constrained properties involving the nonincreasing behavior of this measure under inverse branches of quasiconformal maps and establish a mass lower bound for one such property in the context of quasiconformal equivalence. Applying this newly defined measure, we provide a distinct proof for the mass nonincreasing property of quasiconformal maps' inverse branches and offer a characterization of quasiconformal and homeomorphism fixed points through the application of this measure to the intersection of a quasiconformal map's graph with its second iterate's graph. Additionally, we present a mass condition representing a homeomorphism between two maps' graphs and a characterization of homographic fixed points defined by the interaction of this condition with a quasiconformal map. The MAVEN mission provides data on Mars, offering a dataset of neutral mass density measurements situated between those of the Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) and Mars Reconnaissance Rover (MRO). This paper details the analysis of gravity wave characteristics in Mars' upper atmosphere, utilizing a dataset derived from neutral mass density variations detected by MAVEN. Wavenumber spectra constructed in both vertical and horizontal directions for this new data were compared with those derived from MGS. In addition to comparing spectral profiles, the authors evaluate the spread of gravity waves in Mars' upper atmosphere through the use of coherent planes. Ultimately, the findings from this study are discussed.

The LHC has recently achieved the production of Ultra-Peripheral Collisions (UPCs) using lead ions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV with the LHC. This research details the production yields of $J/\psi$ mesons within these ultraperipheral collisions. The data aligns well with theoretical predictions for $p$-$p$ interactions as observed at the LHC and also matches $p$-$p$ data from $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 2.76$ TeV collected by the ALICE detector. This result offers valuable insights into how such systems approach more central collisions.

This study presents an investigation into using visual input to steer the audio creation process, centered on a system capable of representing audio concepts, generating sound, and creating views of the audio landscape for interactive exploration. Defined are various interactions for manipulating these representations, including direct adjustments to parameters and the selection of node states within a signal flow or the activation of semantic tags. These manipulations influence how the audio concept is rendered to produce varying outputs. Furthermore, the activation of specific semantic tags can modify the signal architecture itself, such as adding or removing nodes in the audio pipeline. Provided is an in-depth analysis of how both the audio structures and their corresponding node states can be edited manually or through automated means. As part of this research, the authors introduced ViPA, a creative tool designed to facilitate visually directed audio production while maintaining a direct mapping between displayed information and actual sound parameters to support intuitive interaction.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are renowned for their ability to capture sequential temporal patterns, yet their performance is constrained by issues such as vanishing gradients and difficulties in learning long-range dependencies. While recent studies suggest that augmenting RNNs with attention heads can enhance these limitations, the specific impact of this modification on different data scales or contexts remains poorly understood. To address this research gap, the paper empirically investigates the effectiveness of both vanilla RNNs and recurrent networks equipped with attention across various scenarios across four practical tasks: sentiment analysis, stock price forecasting, human action recognition, and disease spread prediction. Empirical findings reveal that although an attention augmentation generally improves model outcomes, the gap in performance between standard RNNs and those utilizing attention is negligible in certain contexts.

To address rapidly spreading epidemics, a precise analytical method predicts outbreaks and enables optimal timing for countermeasure implementation. When applied to a representative rapid-response protocol, a unique global stationary distribution characterizes the long-term outburst dynamics, serving as a crucial basis for minimizing infection-related fatalities while balancing economic losses. Extending this approach to a specific containment strategy yields clear first-order conditions that determine the ideal response schedule for achieving both objectives efficiently. These findings are further formalized through an explicit optimization criterion. Numerical analysis across various parametric configurations demonstrates that the conditions establish sufficient and necessary criteria for a global optimum, with the proposed method outperforming non-data-driven heuristics such as perpetual lockdowns, relaxed measures, and circular quarantine in saving lives and protecting the economy.

This article addresses the challenge of diagn issues within machine learning pipelines that integrate both data sources and complex transformations, especially when performance problems stem from troubleshooting across multiple interconnected components. Our specific focus is on identifying data-related troubles in the presence of other issues to enable timely corrections. Our approach, named SSA (Significance Analysis), employs the Shapley value concept to quantify each data component's influence on the model outcome by evaluating its impact on the overall feature significance. SSA is particularly suited for workflows involving complex joins across numerous components, where maintaining precise data lineage proves difficult. By analyzing the local evidence provided by these joined datasets, our method can pinpoint the exact data components responsible for the model's problematic features. We have implemented SSA on a real-world industrial case study involving three petrochemical plants, successfully validating its efficacy in a productional setting.

During the past ten years, significant advances have occurred across multiple domains of algebraic geometry, including enumerative theory. These theoretical leaps have notably reduced the gap between enumerative geometry and other subjects such as combinatorics and topology. Consequently, enumerative theory now frequently employs rigorous principles shared by these related fields to address fundamental problems. Consequently, this presentation aims to provide an accessible introduction for researchers in topology, combinatorics, and other statistical fields by exploring the recent convergence. Focusing on two pivotal problems in enumerative theory—those involving curves within algebraic varieties and singular enumerative geometry—the text will utilize linear systems, Gr\"obner bases, and deformation methods as primary tools to illustrate these theoretical connections.

This study investigates Mn3sn using first-principles calculations, focusing on how pressure affects its hexagonal antiferromagnetic ground state and anomalous Hall effect (AHE). At equilibrium, the system exhibits a spiral antiferromagnetic arrangement with a large negative Hall resistivity, primarily driven by the Berry curvature concentrated on the Fermi surface. Along the c-axis, the lattice constant expansion suppresses the Berry curvature contribution from flat bands, resulting in reduced Hall resistivity. Along the a-axis (in-plane), such expansion promotes hybridization between Fermi surfaces and flat bands along the b direction; this enhances the Berry curvature and increases AHE. Along the a-axis compression similarly strengthens flat band hybridization and boosts AHE, whereas compression along the b-axis elevates the energy of flat bands, diminishing the overall effect. Flat band interactions emerge from Mn d orbitals across different sublattices, where their height is governed by the a-axis length. A similar pattern holds along the b-axis, yet due to shorter distances between layers, interplane interactions significantly exceed those between adjacent unit cells, accounting for anisotropic AHE. These findings offer critical insights into manipulating the AHE in Mn3sn and similar materials via structural engineering.

This paper introduces an overview of the techniques employed in recent Rule-based Relation Extraction (REE) frameworks, with particular focus on end-to-end and multi-task approaches utilizing deep neural networks (DNN). REE aims to identify relational information between pairs of entities across various textual domains, finding applications in knowledge graph expansion, question answering, and text mining. While the discussion addresses the evolution from traditional methods through the integration of DNNs in REE—emphasizing multi-task architectures designed to leverage auxiliary DNNs for enhanced relational inference—it also highlights existing challenges and the direction for future research.

The Steklov problem focuses on determining an eigenvalue associated with an indicator field of the shape within a domain. However, when considering eigenfields that vanish inside the shape, this problem transitions into the Neumann problem, a scenario where eigenvalues coincide with those of the Laplacian in those shapes enclosed. By introducing variations to the Steklov problem by implementing the Robin boundary condition, we can establish results demonstrating that these modifications allow us to decouple coincident eigenfields of different orders, thus producing new, distinct Steklov characteristics that decrease in magnitude as the domain under consideration shrinks.

Although mixed-integer programming with single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotype panels has proven effective at predicting unobserved genotypes in this problem, introducing extra information via "guides" is expected to boost the recovery's precision. We enhance these mixed-integer formulations by integrating linear programming models for graph signaling, resulting in new, more potent inequalities that closely match the true data structure. Specifically, we combine the connectivity of samples with information on genetic variants, resulting in hypergraph-based graphs. Our approach is tested using real 1000 Genomes Project data, where adding the graph constraints to mixed-integer programs consistently and significantly improves solution quality.

Medical imaging forms the cornerstone of clinical practice, yet digital radiographs remain constrained by a lack of standardized, computable structural annotations. This study presents detailed annotations for 1,000 children's chest X-rays (Child's ABPE-1k dataset), capturing both anatomical features and imaging artifacts. The data includes high-precision boundaries for 18 organs/tissues—such as the heart, lungs, and diaphragm—along with 8 common pathologies and 8 CT-derived signal processing artifacts like blurring, ghosting, attenuation correction bands, and motion blur. Developed using "CT projection," this methodology integrates automated detection algorithms with expert radiologist verification to produce training datasets optimized for analysis and interpretation. We evaluated the dataset by comparing the area under the curve (AUC) of quantitative metrics against the results of state-of-the-art segmentation models, including V-Net and DeepLabv3+.

We introduce a novel function, designated as the Thurston norm, which characterizes the minimal Euler characteristic count of any minimal surface belonging to a specific homology class. We then investigate this function in relation to contact frameworks. Our primary finding establishes that for a given contact framework, there exists a minimal surface whose surface of sections achieves equality with our newly defined norm. We further provide a computational formula determining the value of this new norm by examining the minimal mean periods of the magnetic flows defined on the contact structure. Ultimately, we utilize these developed tools to enhance the estimation of the maximal Euler characteristic found among any surface that satisfies the condition of being strictly convex.

This study applies the concept of economic consistency to cryptocurrency exchange rates, specifically examining five leading cryptocurrencies—Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin, Ripple, and Everscoin—as pairs traded against US dollars using data from the LinkedIn platform. By implementing an eigenvalue-based approach within a Two-Stage Fuzzy Relational Data model, this research highlights the inherent cost inconsistencies inherent in cryptocurrency exchanges and introduces a novel methodology for constructing consistent exchange rates based on pairwise comparisons. The investigation reveals an inherent inconsistency level of 5.6% among these five cryptocurrencies.

The one-dimensional Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation governs the growth of randomly evolving surfaces and serves as a universal descriptor for far-from-equilibrium physical systems. Its significance stems from the fact that surfaces develop, on average, perpendicularly to time, generating a strong inherent signal that typically overwhelms faint experimental signatures of far-end time data. However, by applying a novel inverse scattering transform to the KPZ-dynamics, we discover a method to extract these weak far-end time data points despite the dominance of the surface height. This technique reverses information flow within far-end time to physically reduce intense gradients and fluctuations, effectively isolating experimentally delicate signals. This study advances utility far-end time extraction in far-end time dynamics and deepens theoretical comprehension of KPZ-scale transitions through explicit demonstration.

Generating high-contrast pulse pairs or a single pulse in the extreme ultraviolet, soft X-ray, and hard X-ray spectral regions is crucial for numerous applications within the field of ultrafast science. We introduce a technique known as "chirp-tapering" that produces a pulsed structure in the time domain, with the temporal width tailored through adjustable parameters including chirp, power, and bandwidth. When we applied this method to a femtosecond Ti:sapphire laser (760 nm), it yielded two distinct pulses separated by 180 fs with a contrast ratio of $10^{-3}$. However, when used with a 10-fs laser source, it yielded either a well-resolved pair of pulses with this contrast or a solitary pulse depending on the experimental settings. Through time- and spectrally resolved measurements, we analyzed the characteristics of these time structures. This approach is particularly advantageous as it simultaneously fragments the original pulse without altering the spectrum.

This study applies tangible optics—a stage-developed approach to simulate flowing currents—to estimate the dynamics of viscous layered shear fluids. We propose an Ott-Sudarshan-type Taylor expansion for vorticity relative to the optical path of an infinitesimal ray, accounting for variable shear and viscosity. Relative to prior work, this extends the methodology by incorporating mass conservation and assuming a viscous fluid. The derived equations for momentum and mass conservation were solved numerically using an iterative scheme. These simulations demonstrate that when an optic evaluates the strength of an imaginary ray within a real viscous shear current to estimate local shear, it yields a more balanced assessment that avoids overestimation compared to physical metrics like vorticity. Furthermore, assuming the ray traverses layers of uniform thickness enables the numerical recovery of layer-by-layer mass flux.

Gerrymandering represents a critical issue in American politics, involving the manipulation of electoral districting boundaries to skew election outcomes without altering voter registration data. While previous research has utilized various computational methods—including Markov chain Monte Carlo, simulated annealing, and evolutionary algorithms—to generate examples or detect such manipulation, this study introduces an approach based on simulated tempering. This method proves exceptionally effective at producing an extensive and diverse set of gerrymandered maps across an vast solution space. Furthermore, this suite of algorithms not only exhibits rapid convergence but also serves as superior for applications in map classification and the visualization of underlying value functions.

Identifying defects in textile images is critical for quality control in the industry. To address this, we introduce a new flow-based approach for flaw detection in regularly spaced fabrics, where local texture features are extracted using Frequent Local Gabor Histogram Oriented Gradient (GLGOH) and input into a matrix representing image patches. To manage storage and computational demands, Low-Rank Subspace Approximation (LRA) performs dimensionality reduction on the matrix stack. Subsequent flaw classification is achieved by applying K-means clustering to the low-rank representations of individual images, with results evaluated using F-measure and average processing times demonstrating that this flow methodology maintains competitive performance. Furthermore, increasing the number of neighboring images incorporated into each matrix enhances both efficiency and classification quality, allowing our approach to match the quality of established non-flow techniques.

This research proposes a new visual navigation framework driven by reinforcement learning and regulated by data-theoretic principles. We integrate an empirical Bayes approach into the agent's reinforcement learning policy, ensuring the balance between exploring the environment and exploiting learned insights. This integration enables more efficient agent learning, reducing reliance on training data. Furthermore, we introduce a novel regularization term into both reward design and observation state transformations, a component calculated via the KL-divergence between prior and posterior distributions. This term enhances the robustness of critical elements within our visual navigation framework, as demonstrated by empirical results where our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in challenging, realistic navigation scenarios.

Collaborative work between humans and robots is increasingly vital for society and the SII sector, driving the need for methods to safely and efficiently share manipulatable objects. This study introduces a system where a human and a robot independently reach across a central object using a "parallel conveyance" approach. Once the object is grasped by both agents simultaneously, a manifold-aware Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm registers the robot's hand trajectory relative to human movement in real-time, effectively transforming the robot's task space into the broader human domain. To facilitate simultaneous grasps, a safety barrier field ensures optimal positioning between the human and robot. Additionally, an optimization strategy minimizes relative distances by leveraging negative Poisson kernel properties, thereby reducing collision risks. Simulation tests and video recordings confirm that this conveyance method enables safe parallel grasps, while the manifold-aware ICP provides precise estimation of the robot's workspace expansion into human territory.

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently gained traction for their ability to model complex real-world phenomena, yet they face obstacles related to computational cost and data set size. To address these issues, this paper introduces Residual-driven Adaptive Node Generation, a method for dynamically adding PINNN nodes during training to specific regions of high uncertainty, as identified by elevated residual values. The approach employs a revised node generation algorithm that evaluates the local environment around each candidate point, ensuring better alignment with physical context compared to uniform alternatives. Furthermore, a new parent-to-child information transfer mechanism has been developed to enhance feature learning efficiency. Extensive numerical tests confirm the method's robustness and efficacy, even under extreme scenarios, such as using only ten input data points per dimension in high-dimensional spaces.

Dual-domain ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs) are designed to leverage the properties of two-body hysteresis through negative capacitance (NC), enabling sub-60 mV/decade transconductance and enhanced energy efficiency. While experimental results on small prototypes have validated these benefits, theoretical models on multi-domain FeFets remain scarce. In this study, we employ a two-scale model to analyze device behavior across lengthscales ranging from hundreds of nanometers down to sub-tens-of-nm. First, a two-state model is used to simulate hysteresis and domain wall dynamics at the coarser scale. Subsequently, these outputs, including domain wall positions, are utilized within a coarser-to-sub-micro model to examine the electric field distribution within individual domains at a higher resolution. Finally, these microscopic field distributions are mapped back via model order reduction techniques to the initial two-state framework, validating domain-wall activity as a critical parameter influencing NC effects at that scale. Ultimately, this hierarchical approach establishes a two-state framework capable of predicting hysteresis dynamics in both physical and electrical regimes of multi-domain devices, paving the way for systematic model order reduction strategies essential for standard compact modeling.

The rapid expansion of the logistics sector has generated substantial interest in designing novel logistics networks. However, ensuring the overall resilience of these emerging ecosystems remains elusive, as standard evaluation methods for fragility are lacking. Consequently, this research introduces a specialized graph approach for fragility analysis specifically tailored to freight ecosystems. The core objective is to assess how the closure of individual nodes impacts the broader network, a process executed by calculating node betweenness to identify critical closures and employing system theory to isolate closed-system characteristics. Furthermore, a novel metric called "Fragility Index" has been developed to quantify the extent of potential failures. The proposed methodology is demonstrated through an analysis of the Hungarian railway network.

This study addresses the establishment of the irreducibility of stochastic intricate Ginzburg-Landau (iGL) equations subject to pure jump noise with infinite variation on a Hilbert space. By assuming linear deterministic parts satisfy specific conditions, the authors prove an open topology irreducibility result for the corresponding stochastic dynamics. Consequently, they derive the existence of a unique stationary distribution under the linear stochastic framework of the continuous stochastic Skempton (SSG) equations perturbed by pure jump noise with infinite variation as a direct application of the main theorem, extending previous work to cases involving pure jump disturbances and an broader class of nonlinear terms compared to prior research focused on continuous noise disturbances on $ \mathbb{T}^1 $.

This paper introduces Orientation Convolutional Networks (OCNs), which are convolutional architectures designed to automatically learn robust orientation-invariant features by integrating specific orientation convolutional layers. Each layer in these networks comprises multiple subunits, where every subunit maintains an invariant weight matrix relative to changes in image rotation, effectively acting as shared filters across different directional shifts. Our experimental results on the MNIST, EMNIST-balanced, and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that OCNs match the accuracy of residual networks but match or exceed standard convolutions in lightweight variants, offering superior matching performance without sacrificing efficiency. Furthermore, we evaluated these networks on the Robust Net task using CIFAR-10, confirming that our models achieve higher precision than conventional three-residual or dense block networks.

Handling 3D object recognition remains a major technical hurdle in computer vision, and this study focuses on processing point clouds through neural networks. While Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have demonstrated exceptional success in the "brain" of other 3D domains, such as surface segmentation, their application in segmenting individual objects has been underexplored. This paper presents the pioneering work of integrating GCNs specifically for single-object segmentation. The proposed method begins by constructing a graph from the point cloud and then employs multi-layer GCNs to extract effective local and global features. Additionally, a dedicated "points-to-graph" module is used to perform dimensional reduction on the resulting feature vectors before feeding them into the network. The resulting models, denoted as multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), are then trained for objective classification. The proposed approach has been validated on the ModelNet40 benchmark, where it achieves a macro average Intersection over Union (mAvG mIoU) of 70.1%, placing it among the top-tier performances reported thus far. The methodology is implemented in the GitHub repository: https://github.com/yzhang0101/GCNet_ObjectSegment.

Computer-based simulations and experimental data in scientific and engineering fields frequently involve time series outputs, such as power spectrum densities, which serve as crucial indicators for characterizing phenomena ranging from fluid dynamics to financial markets. Accurantly inferring the underlying parameters of these models from such data is vital for assessing and enhancing system performance. However, the simultaneous assessment of numerous possible parameter sets remains difficult, particularly when the data consists of noisy time series corrupted by random variability. This paper introduces a novel Bayesian framework for parameter inference using contoured set-valued probabilistic regression (CSVS) on time series data. This approach treats parameters as a set and determines the most probable range by analyzing their posterior probability distribution. To effectively address the uncertainty inherent in noisy data, a dedicated convergence criterion has been developed to efficiently filter parameters, ensuring only those with significant posterior probability are retained. Additionally, a computationally practical method was created to determine appropriate parameters for various set-valued computational models. Validation of this methodology occurred through the analysis of turbulent flow data from wind tunnels and numerical large-eddy flow simulations. Finally, an accurate contour set-valued probabilistic regression (CSVS) technique was applied to estimate flow field characteristics and relevant parameters, successfully inferring key metrics such as turbulent kinetic energy and the scale of turbulent length.

The core premise of Regional Query (RQ) methods is that a client can recover a global model by aggregating query responses sent by other clients. While prior research showed RQs facilitate efficient large-scale federated learning (FL), their impact on resilience against malicious actors has not been thoroughly explored. This work investigates how RQs impact the ability of FL to survive attacks. Our findings reveal a counterintuitive result: although querying multiple regions might seem to gather more data, the queried clients often send highly similar models, offering little additional value compared to receiving inputs from a single region. Moreover, because RQs increase the attack surface by exposing more model parameters to external queries, they actually make the system more vulnerable to malicious attacks. Consequently, our results highlight that FL with RQs can be less resilient than standard FL in the presence of bad actors.

Thermodynamic modeling, which incorporates the thermal muon chemical potential and thermal $\eta$ chemical potential components of hadron production, is employed. The study compares theoretical model results with experimental data to explore how the equation of state (EOS) of the quark-gluon plasma behaves under varying conditions.

Parton distribution functions bridge the gap between perturbative and perturbative quantum chromodynamics. We explore efficient methodologies for interpolating and advancing these functions across energy scales. Our analysis compares the performance of several approaches, including a new algorithm developed for logarithmic advancement, and all methods are illustrated using the HERAPDF 2.0 dataset.

Sintered agglomerates, which are prevalent in both lunar and Martian environments, offer valuable insights into the thermal histories and heat flow characteristics of these celestial bodies. However, such agglomerates are rare in smaller satellites like the moons of Mars and large asteroids, suggesting more intense past thermal activity. While some of these clumps may result from impact thermal spikes, others likely stem from volcanic emissions. To better understand their diverse origins, we examined how thermal aggregation affects the structural and mechanical properties of simulated regolith for both Mars and the Moon, using 106-μm glass beads as a lunar proxy and incorporating quartz powder to mimic Martian conditions. By applying various mass ratios and saturation temperature points, we evaluated the mechanics of the resulting agglomerates through three-point bending tests. Additionally, high-resolution scanning electron microscopy was utilized to observe microstructures. Our findings indicate that the properties of these clumps are heavily dependent on aggregate size and saturation temperature, with a proposed mechanism linking small-agglomerate failure to bead fracture and large-agglomerate failure to bead separation. These structures were further compared to actual samples collected from the Apollo missions (lunar) and potential future Martian expeditions. This research underscores how analyzing sintered regolith can reveal critical information about ancient thermal events.

When a horizontal jet of liquid drops into an air environment, its surface undergoes Rayleigh-plateau instability, eventually breaking apart into uniform droplets. Conversely, when this jet encloses another type of fluid within a coaxial shell, internal coat disturbances can occur in the jet. These coats may experience slip if they interact with jets having matching viscosities or if they enclose air, which allows for energy transfer via instability modes. However, if a liquid settles on an external fiber, it initially forms a cylindrical shape aligned with the surface before undergoing slip-enhanced instability similar to that seen in jets. Our investigation focuses on this specific case of a drop coated on a fiber, analyzing how slip at the interface influences growth rates and mode numbers for cylindrical disturbances. We utilize a model that maps this configuration onto an equivalent free-falling jet to predict slip effects. Validating our approach with experimental data for both drops and jets confirms that this mapping is accurate. Additionally, we validate predictions by comparing our results to experiments involving hydrophobic fibers, which clearly show the predicted impact of slip on instability characteristics in that environment.

This study examines this link by using the $\lambda$2.42$\mu$m benchmark SFR indicator, the Brackett-$\gamma$ line, in 12118 cases. Our sample comprises 1.12 million galaxies observed by the Hubble Space Telescope, with constituting spectral data from the James Webb Space Telescope. This is supported by 1.12 million galaxies observed with the HST and support data from the JWST. Robust and efficient distributional robustness testing has emerged as a critical requirement for a wide variety of practical applications. To address this, researchers have developed diverse solutions, predominantly relying on the Wasserstein metric, a strategy known thus far for yielding suboptimal performance. This study introduces Unique, a novel framework that achieves U(niqueness) in robust testing through unique approaches. The core of this method involves employing a unified representation of probability measures via optimal transport so as to simplify calculations, while simultaneously introducing a new family of metrics called the Generalized Quasi-Wasserstein (QGW), which offers greater flexibility than the traditional Wasserstein metric. Comprehensive experimental evaluations across numerous datasets indicate that Qu UW outclasses other state-of-the-art algorithms in both accuracy and computational speed. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/jianjianjiang/Unique.

Recognizing handwritten mathematical formulas is vital for enabling interactive mathematical tools that support learning and education; however, current formula identification research has primarily relied on non-natural pen strokes and a limited variety of expressions. This study utilizes $90$ distinct formula images, including more than $30$ unique formulas, and a high-precision reference system to evaluate performance, thereby improving the accuracy of mathematical formula recognition. Additionally, we propose two $\text{Convolutional Neural Network}$ architectures tailored for this task, which achieve state-of-the-art results. Finally, the evaluation process includes a fine-grained analysis of the data, demonstrating a high correlation between the physical writing dynamics and the trajectory of pen

Although the primary objective of speech length normalization is often seen as a pre-processing step for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), it can also improve Noisy Speech-Speech Translation (NSS-ST). This study examines how far non-statistical methods can go in addressing Asymmetric Speech Length Normalization (ASLN). We propose a straightforward yet underutilized technique that aligns synthetic source lengths with actual reference lengths using median-based sampling. Because the method relies solely on source and reference alignment—without using statistical or cross-statistical matching—it does not constitute a standard ASLN approach. However, it effectively delivers comparable performance to leading statistical assays in the ASLN domain. Experiments demonstrate a ~10% relative reduction in Word Error Rate on the Switchboard-2 test set using -tri2- & -trans- language models.

Multi-dimensional data characterized as presence/absence or count information frequently arise in ecological and epidemiological research. While various statistical models address these datasets using covariates, spatially referenced data demand specialized approaches that account for spatial dependence, a trait often indicative of underlying biological or ecological processes. This requirement has prompted the development of numerous spatial modeling frameworks applicable to single-species data or designed for joint analysis of multiple species, some of which incorporate additional information from independent sampling studies. The `spHabitat` R package provides implementations for these diverse models, including those with linear and nonlinear continuous predictors, and supports both Bayesian and maximum likelihood estimation through the flexible infrastructure of the modern modeling package **brms**.

The DermoCancer initiative is dedicated to addressing skin lesions and cancer, with current efforts focused on diagnosing cancerous lesions. We introduce the DermoCancer Skin Care project, which aims to leverage deep learning for the detection and differential diagnosis of these lesions. This effort utilizes a publicly available dataset containing 20,678 dermoscopic images sourced from the 2018 and 2019 versions of the International Skin Lesion Challenge (ISIC 2018/2019). Our current tool achieves 80.5% accuracy on the test set when comparing benign versus malignant classifications. This result surpasses the performance observed in the Challenge submissions and nearly matches leading entries from other participants who achieved nearly identical accuracy rates. We further demonstrate the model's efficacy through evaluations on external datasets, including ISIC 2019 and B3-AAD, as well as benchmarking against previous submissions from other teams. Additionally, we describe the underlying solution and present future aspirations for the project.

This study utilizes a multi-dimensional stochastic autoencoder (SAE) to analyze multi-wavelength spectral time-series data from the Gold Sample (comprising 1,762 SNe Ia) from the Pantheon dataset. The SNE Ia cases are first classified into three distinct groups based on their discovery method. Subsequently, we examine the chaotic and disordered nature of these spectra within both time and wavelength domains. Finally, using the trained SAE SNe Ia are classified into three groups with a high recovery rate of 92%, effectively learning the complex and disordered nature of these spectra within both time and wavelength domains. We have identified and characterized the neutral resonance line (res) spectra of a galaxy rich in star formation and exhibiting strong gravitational lensing at a redshift of z = 2.09, observed with the VLT/UVES. The emission profile reveals multiple kinematic components, the majority showing velocity dispersions exceeding 500 km s$^{-1}$ that likely stem from massive, young stellar clusters. However, one distinct component displays a spatial extent corresponding to a physical scale of approximately 2 kpc and a velocity dispersion under 100 km s$^{-1}$, suggesting it originates from the interstellar medium within a lensed lens. When compared with UV continuum predictions and other ionized lines, the ratios of res luminosity are generally high, implying that the interstellar medium is ionization-bounded.
